title: The Quarter We Can See
hook: the whole world, every star and ant, is one quarter of the cosmic person. why hindus see god in nature without calling nature all of god
carry: god fills the world and is still more
tomorrow: what was the world made from?

segments.voice: Yesterday, god is in all this, every face included opened: a person with a thousand heads, covering the earth and standing beyond it by ten fingers' width.
screen: `A THOUSAND HEADS, AND TEN FINGERS MORE.`

segments.voice: Someone you've worked beside for years, the one who fixes the printer and remembers birthdays, stands up at a wedding and sings. The room goes quiet, because the voice is extraordinary. You had no idea. You knew a real part of this person, nothing fake about it. But it was a part, and not the larger one. The Purusha Sukta's third verse does something like that with the whole world. It takes everything that exists, every star and ant and city, and says: this is the part of him you've met.
screen: `THE COWORKER WHO FIXES THE PRINTER.` → `THEN SHE SINGS.` → `YOU'D ONLY MET A PART.`

segments.voice: Verse three: such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still. Then a proportion. Pado asya vishva bhutani. A quarter of him is all beings. Pada means a foot, and also a quarter. Everything that lives and dies is one quarter. Three quarters of him, the verse says, are immortal, in heaven. Verse four goes on. With three quarters the Purusha rose up. The one quarter came to be here, again and again, and from it he spread out into what eats and what doesn't: the hungry sparrow and the stone. So the world, for all its size, is the smaller share. Every galaxy, every person, is truly his, and still only the part that came down. Later Hindu texts keep this shape. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna he holds up this whole universe with a single fragment of himself. Scholars sometimes call this panentheism: everything is in God, and God is more than everything. It's why a Hindu can bow to a river, a tree, a cow, a teacher, and still pray to a God no river could hold. So if someone says Hindus just worship nature, the oldest layer of the Veda answers: nature is sacred because it's his, and it's the quarter we can see.
screen: `SUCH IS HIS GREATNESS, AND MORE.` · `PADA: A FOOT, A QUARTER.` · `ALL BEINGS ARE ONE QUARTER.` · `IN GOD, AND GOD IS MORE.`

segments.voice: Look at one living thing near you, a plant, a pet, the sky in a window, or picture one. Let it be sacred, part of the quarter that came down, and touch your hands together toward it. Then close your eyes and rest in what's beyond it, the three quarters no eye has seen. If you pray, pray to the One who is more; if you don't, simply rest in the more.
The Purusha Sukta. In its third and fourth verses, all beings are one quarter of the Purusha, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.
Your line: God fills the world, and is still more. The whole world is the quarter that came down. Until tomorrow.

what a scholar hears: pado 'sya vishva bhutani tripad asyamritam divi, where pada is both 'foot' and 'quarter', and the Gita's 'a single fragment' (10.42) echoes the same shape.

notes: Sanskrit from memory: 3a etāvān asya mahimā ato jyāyāṃś ca pūruṣaḥ; 3c–d pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripād asyāmṛtaṃ divi (written open as pado asya vishva bhutani). Confirm.

Paraphrase of 10.90.4 (tripād ūrdhva ud ait puruṣaḥ pādo 'syehābhavat punaḥ, tato viṣvaṅ vy akrāmat sāśanānaśane abhi): 'came to be here again and again' renders punaḥ; 'what eats and what doesn't eat' renders sāśanānaśane; the gloss 'the living and the lifeless' is interpretive. Confirm.
Pada as foot / quarter, with the four-legged-animal explanation, is a common gloss; confirm.
Gita 10.42 paraphrased (viṣṭabhyāham idaṃ kṛtsnam ekāṃśena sthito jagat); the link to the Purusha Sukta is presented as a rhyme, not as a claim that the Gita quotes it.
